rendered:
The micropores are about ∼0.5 nm[1], as verified by FFT analysis of TEM images. The pores are too small to take in the electrolyte solvent molecule, which is ∼0.7 nm in diameter[2], so the solvent cannot enter. The sodium ion is much smaller, only ∼0.2 nm in diameter[3]. Because the ion cannot carry its solvent shell into the pores, it must shed that shell at the outer surface of the microporous host and then travel into the carbon on its own to reach the sulfur. The reaction therefore runs as a quasi solid-state process at the cathode, rather than as a conversion reaction in which ions move through the electrolyte to an active site before desolvating.
